entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Christopher II of Denmark was King of Denmark from 1320 to 1326 and again from 1329 until his death in 1332. He was a younger son of Eric V and played a significant role in the dissolution of the Danish state during his reign.

Christopher II's rule was marked by a series of calamities, including a devastating flood in 1325 and a plague that killed thousands of Danes. The kingdom's economy was also in shambles, with heavy taxes and a crippling debt.

The near-total collapse of the Danish state during Christopher II's reign led to a period of fragmentation and power struggles among the nobility. This, in turn, paved the way for the rise of the Kalmar Union, a political entity that united Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a single ruler.

In the end, Christopher II's legacy was one of ruin and devastation, a stark reminder of the fragility of even the most powerful kingdoms.

This statement can be summed up in the words of the 14th-century historian, 'The king's downfall was a result of his own folly and the treachery of his subjects.'
